toc.title: Agent Architecture: Loops, Supervisors and Subagents

html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. SDK: software development kit; API: application programming interface

  • Workflow versus agent: the decision criteria
  • Manager and supervisor hierarchies and the role of subagents
  • The common agent patterns: tool-use loop, subagents, memory, context-window management
  • The common workflow patterns: chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer
  • Agentic frameworks (Strands, LangGraph, PydanticAI) and when to use one

2Workflow or Agent?

Running case

Tidewater Automates Claim Intake

  • Step list today: read the claim email, extract the policy number, check coverage, draft a reply
  • Some claims are odd: missing data, several policies, unclear damage
  • The team asks: "Do we need an agent, or just a workflow?"
Workflow Agent
Control Your code defines the path (fixed or branching steps) The model decides the next step in a loop with tools
Predictability High: same steps, testable, cheaper Lower: flexible, harder to test
Fits Well-understood tasks with known steps Open-ended tasks where the steps depend on what is found
Cost and latency Lower, bounded Higher, variable (many model calls)

  • Decision criteria: predictability of the steps, complexity, cost and latency budget, tolerance for errors, and need for auditing.
  • Start with the simplest thing that works: one good prompt, then a workflow, then an agent. Add autonomy only when the simpler design fails the evals.
  • Many real systems are workflows with one agentic step (for example a fixed intake pipeline that hands odd cases to an agent).
Exam tip

"Steps are known and must be reliable and cheap" → workflow. "The path depends on what the task discovers" → agent.

3Workflow Patterns

Pattern Use it when Claims example
Prompt chaining A task splits into fixed sequential steps Extract fields, then check coverage, then draft the reply
Routing Inputs fall into categories that need different handling Route "auto" and "property" claims to different prompts or models
Parallelization Independent subtasks, or the same task several times for confidence Review ten documents at once; vote on a coverage decision
Orchestrator-workers The subtasks cannot be predicted in advance A planner splits a large claim file into parts for workers
Evaluator-optimizer A clear quality criterion exists and iteration improves the result Draft a reply, critique it against a checklist, revise
Exam tip

A fixed pipeline with one hard case is usually a workflow with an agentic step, not a fully autonomous agent.

4Agent Architecture: Loops, Supervisors and Subagents

  • Tool-use loop (the core agent pattern): send the request, the model returns tool_use, your code runs the tool and returns the result, repeat until end_turn (see the loop in the Architect course; here it is a pattern to recognize).
  • Manager or supervisor hierarchy: a supervisor agent breaks a goal into tasks, delegates to subagents, collects results and decides what is next.
  • Why subagents improve task execution:
    • Context isolation: verbose work stays in the subagent's own context window; only a summary returns
    • Specialization: a focused prompt and a small tool set per role
    • Parallelism: independent subagents run at the same time
  • Memory: short-term is the conversation in the context window; long-term is stored outside the model (files, a database, a memory tool) and loaded when relevant.
  • Context-window management: prune tool output, summarize or compact, delegate to subagents (Module 9).

5Agentic Frameworks

Framework What it is Typical reason to choose it
Claude Agent SDK The agent loop and tools behind Claude Code, as a library You want Claude's own harness: tools, subagents, hooks, sessions
Strands Agents A model-driven agent framework (strong AWS integration) Building agents with tools on AWS with little code
LangGraph Stateful graphs of nodes and edges for multi-step workflows Explicit control flow, branching, persistence and human-in-the-loop steps
PydanticAI An agent framework built around typed, validated outputs (Pydantic models) Strongly typed structured outputs and validation
  • Framework or direct API? A framework gives faster development, patterns and state handling; the cost is abstraction (you see less of the prompts and calls), extra dependencies and the need to understand what runs underneath. Use the plain API for simple flows and when you need full control.
  • Whatever you pick, you still need evals, logging and guardrails; a framework does not replace them.
Exam tip

Pick a framework for the specific capability it offers (state graph, typed output, Claude's own harness); do not pick one just because it is popular.

6Exam Q&A

S1The steps of Tidewater's invoice check are always the same: extract fields, validate totals, write a summary. Reliability and low cost matter. What fits best?

  • AA single huge prompt with no validation
  • BA fully autonomous agent with every tool and no fixed steps
  • CA supervisor with ten subagents
  • DA workflow (prompt chain) with fixed steps
Show the answer

Answer: D. Known, fixed steps call for a workflow, which is more predictable and cheaper than an agent.

S2An investigation task has no fixed steps: what to check next depends on what the previous check found. Which design suits it?

  • AA cron job
  • BA hard-coded sequence of five prompts
  • CA single prompt with all facts pasted in
  • DAn agent that decides the next step in a tool-use loop
Show the answer

Answer: D. When the path depends on discoveries, the model must choose the next step.

S3Incoming claims fall into auto, property and liability categories, each needing a different prompt. Which pattern fits?

  • ARouting: classify, then send to the matching handler
  • BEvaluator-optimizer
  • CParallelization of the same prompt over every claim at once
  • DPrompt chaining only
Show the answer

Answer: A. Routing sends inputs of different types to specialized handling.

S4A developer wants an answer drafted, then critiqued against a checklist and revised until it passes. Which pattern is this?

  • AOrchestrator-workers
  • BRouting
  • CEvaluator-optimizer
  • DParallelization
Show the answer

Answer: C. Generate, evaluate against criteria, and iterate is the evaluator-optimizer pattern.

S5A large claim file must be split into parts that cannot be known ahead of time, each handled by a worker. Which pattern is this?

  • ARouting the claim to a specialist handler by category
  • BOrchestrator-workers
  • CPrompt chaining
  • DA single call
Show the answer

Answer: B. An orchestrator plans dynamic subtasks and delegates them to workers.

S6Why use subagents in a supervisor design?

  • ASubagents share one context window
  • BEach has its own context window and focused tools; only summaries return
  • CSubagents are free of charge
  • DSubagents remove the need for evals because every subagent tests its own work
Show the answer

Answer: B. Isolation, specialization and parallelism improve task execution and keep the supervisor's context small.

S7An agent must remember customer preferences across many sessions. What is the right place for long-term memory?

  • AThe system prompt, edited by hand every day by the team that runs the agent
  • BA store outside the model (files, a database or a memory tool) loaded when relevant
  • COnly the context window
  • DThe model's weights
Show the answer

Answer: B. Context windows are per request; durable memory belongs in external storage.

S8A team needs explicit state, branching and human approval steps in a multi-step workflow. Which kind of framework fits?

  • AA spreadsheet
  • BNo framework is ever suitable
  • CA stateful graph framework such as LangGraph
  • DA framework that hides all control flow
Show the answer

Answer: C. Stateful graph frameworks model nodes, edges and persisted state explicitly.

S9Which TWO are good reasons to prefer the plain API over a framework? Select TWO.

  • AThe flow is simple and you want full control of prompts and calls
  • BA framework is always cheaper to run
  • CFrameworks guarantee correct answers
  • DYou want to avoid extra dependencies
  • EFrameworks make evals unnecessary
Show the answer

Answer: A, D. Simple flows and a small dependency footprint favor the plain API; frameworks do not remove the need for evals or guarantee correctness.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Workflow vs agent Workflow = your code sets the path; agent = the model decides in a loop
Choose Known steps → workflow; open-ended → agent; start simple
Workflow patterns Chaining · routing · parallelization · orchestrator-workers · evaluator-optimizer
Subagents Context isolation · specialization · parallelism; summaries return
Memory Short-term = context window; long-term = external store
Frameworks Claude Agent SDK · Strands · LangGraph (stateful graphs) · PydanticAI (typed outputs)
Framework tradeoff Speed and patterns vs abstraction and dependencies; evals still required
